```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
devtools::load_all(".")
```

For tutorial purposes, SCCNVis comes with example inputs. We will begin by
loading them and giving a brief summary of what is in each of them. Note that
the length of `cell.names` is equal to the number of rows in `input.matrix`
and that the length of `granges` is equal to the number of columns in the
`input.matrix`.

```{r setup}
library(SCCNVis)

set.seed(42)

#Example input matrix
input.matrix <- example.matrix
print(dim(input.matrix))

#Example cell names
cell.names <- example.cells
print(length(cell.names))
print(cell.names[1:3])

#Example GenomicRanges::GRanges obect
granges <- example.granges
print(granges)

#Example metadata data.frame object
meta.df <- example.meta
print(head(meta.df))

#Create a SCCNVis object
obj <- SCCNVis::createPlotObject(input.matrix, cell.names, granges, meta.df)
```


The SCCNVis object is a simple object. It contains the input matrix (accessible
as `obj@Matrix`) and the associated GenomicRanges::GRanges object (accessible as
`obj@GRanges`). It also contains metadata associated with each cell, if provided.
All plotting functions withing SCCNVis use this object as input.

For example, a simple heatmap can be created using the following:

```{r}
heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj)
print(names(heatmap.result))
print(names(heatmap.result$PlotData))
```

As you can see, the result is a list object that contains the `Plot`, which is
a `ComplexHeatmap` object, and the `PlotData`. In this case, the `PlotData`
is a list containing the actual PlotData (a matrix for the heatmap) and a clustering
result, which relates to the row ordering in the heatmap. In this case, it also
includes the information for drawing the legend of the plot. These values can be used
to create other version of the plot using other packages, or be saved for downstream 
analysis. 

The resulting file can be saved however you would normally export a `ComplexHeatmap`.
For convenience, it can be saved using the SCCNVis wrapper function for exporting plots.
The expected output for the heatmap is also shown below.
```{r eval=FALSE}
#Example manual method
#png("output/file.png", width=2000, height=500)
#ComplexHeatmap::draw(heatmap.result$Plot,
#     show_heatmap_legend = FALSE,
#     annotation_legend_list = heatmap.result$PlotData$Legend)
#dev.off()

#Simple wrapper for convenience
SCCNVis::saveCustomPlot(heatmap.result, "/path/to/heatmap.png")
```

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example 1a. Heatmap", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("1a_heatmap.png")
```

The heatmap could be further customized if metadata has been provided. At the same
time, we may choose to limit our plot to specific regions of interest. For this
example, we may choose to focus only on chr7 and chrX, as seen below:

```{r}
plot.regions <- example.granges[example.granges@seqnames == "chr7" |
                                  example.granges@seqnames == "chrX",]

heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj,
                                         gr = plot.regions,
                                         annotations = "Sample",
                                         show.annotation.name = TRUE,
                                         annotation.colors = list(
                                           Sample = c("SampleA" = "red",
                                                      "SampleB" = "blue")
                                         ))
```
```{r echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example 1b. Heatmap of chr7 and chrX, with sample annotation", out.width = '50%'}
knitr::include_graphics("1b_heatmap.png")
```

We can see that there are at least 2 seemingly distinct clusters present in our heatmap. 
To simplify our heatmap, we may wish to present the data as a simple 
average of those groups. To do so, we must add metadata to the SCCNVis object
to assign each cell to a group, then tell the makeSCHeatmap function which 
metadata column to group the cells by. Whenever the heatmap is the result of
grouped data, the right side of the plot will show the number of cells 
described by each group.

```{r}
#Calculate distance matrix values
dist <- parallelDist::parallelDist(obj@Matrix)
#Perform hierarchical clustering
hc_re <- hclust(dist, method="ward.D2")
#Split the hierarchical clustering into two groups
kclusters <- cutree(hc_re, k = 2)
obj <- SCCNVis::addMetaData(obj, kclusters, colname = "KClusters")


heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj,
                                         group = "KClusters")
```
```{r echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example 1c. Heatmap with pre-specified clusters", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("1c_heatmap.png")
```

Alternatively, you may create groups using any other method you choose, such
as sample of origin, phenotype data, or dynamic clusters. In this example,
I use the dynamicTreeCut package to dynamically cluster the cells and group
the heatmap using the resulting clusters. I am interested in what proportion
of each dynamic cluster comes from each sample, so I set the `secondary.group`
as the `Sample` metadata column

```{r}
dynamic.kclusters <- dynamicTreeCut::cutreeDynamic(dendro = hc_re, 
                                                   distM = as.matrix(dist),
                                                   deepSplit = 0,
                                                   pamRespectsDendro = TRUE
                                                   )
names(dynamic.kclusters) <- hc_re$labels
obj <- SCCNVis::addMetaData(obj, dynamic.kclusters, colname = "DynamicKClusters")

heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj,
                                         group = "DynamicKClusters",
                                         secondary.group = "Sample")
```
```{r echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Example 1d. Heatmap with dynamic clusters", out.width = '100%'}
knitr::include_graphics("1d_heatmap.png")
```
